strengths: The paper contributes a useful, NLP-relevant resource: 20,281 preference pairs derived from naturally occurring conversational feedback, plus model-specific variants. Connecting feedback extraction, response generation, and preference training is a practical contribution.

Training utility is supported across three model families and three established benchmarks, beyond the proposed checklist evaluator. For example, Phi-3 with WF GPT-4 improves AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate from 24.3% to 34.9% and Arena-Hard from 15.4% to 32.4%. Regenerating UltraFeedback responses provides a meaningful contemporary baseline.

The authors conduct human validation on 50 conversations for feedback detection and 200 for checklist evaluation. DSAT precision of 83.3% supports the usefulness of the extracted signals. Reported separation of training and test users and conversations is also appropriate.

The manuscript clearly explains the pipeline and supplies a public dataset link, annotation rubrics, prompts, model versions, and substantial training details. The documented resource and demonstrated training utility support a Findings recommendation, although the broader alignment claims are less secure.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of actual user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, and preference-pair construction. A baseline using the same WildChat prompts with generic response improvement, together with removed or shuffled feedback, would establish whether feedback itself produces the gains. An SFT-only comparison would also clarify the contribution of preference optimization.

The claimed superior validity of checklist evaluation is insufficiently established. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and evaluates outputs using those extracted preferences. Increased wins after supplying the checklist therefore do not independently establish better alignment with users. Human validation helps, but agreement is only 57.14% with κ=0.372, and the study does not compare checklist and ordinary judging against the same human judgments or independently validate the extracted preference summaries.

The evaluation supports a restricted population claim. The 540-item test set deliberately selects central preferences within 70 clusters and tasks similar to training tasks; this does not establish representativeness of the broader user population. DSAT recall is only 48.4%, further limiting feedback coverage. The acknowledged selection bias and continued dependence on model judgments warrant narrower claims about diverse user preferences and reduced bias.

Claims of consistent and significant superiority over UltraFeedback exceed the evidence. Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 underperforms its UF counterpart on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66); other configurations also lose on raw win rate. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and variation across training runs are absent, leaving several small comparative gains uncertain.

Reconstructing the dataset and custom evaluation is less fully specified than retraining the models. Missing details include the embedding model and similarity procedure used for test selection, data-generation decoding settings, and the operational procedure for enforcing user-disjoint splits. These omissions limit exact reproducibility despite the useful dataset release and training documentation.
